articles.title: Hateco and APM Terminals explore Vietnam rail freight network
articles.summary: Hateco Group and APM Terminals have signed a Memorandum of Understanding to study the investment, development and operation of railway freight terminals in Vietnam. The agreement was signed on 20 October 2026 in Denmark during the Vietnam–Denmark Business Forum. The ceremony took place during the State visit of...
articles.body: Hateco Group and APM Terminals have signed a Memorandum of Understanding to study the investment, development and operation of railway freight terminals in Vietnam. The agreement was signed on 20 October 2026 in Denmark during the Vietnam–Denmark Business Forum. The ceremony took place during the State visit of General Secretary and President To Lam and was witnessed by senior representatives from both countries. APM Terminals is part of A.P. Moller – Maersk. The non-binding agreement expands the cooperation between Hateco and APM Terminals from container port infrastructure to railway connectivity and multimodal logistics. Railway freight terminal planned in Hai Phong Under the MOU, the companies will jointly study and propose the development and operation of a railway freight terminal in Hai Phong. The proposed facility would include a cargo-handling centre and storage yards. Hateco and APM Terminals will also examine three additional railway freight locations in northern Vietnam. The proposed network would connect industrial parks, manufacturing centres and logistics hubs with the country’s seaports. The facilities are expected to use digital technology for cargo reception, management, storage and transshipment. If developed, the network would support container movements between northern Vietnam’s industrial areas, Hai Phong’s port system and international shipping routes. The parties expect the proposed connections to improve transport efficiency, reduce pressure on road infrastructure and support Vietnam’s import and export supply chains. Cooperation extends beyond port infrastructure The railway initiative follows the cooperation between Hateco and APM Terminals at Hateco Hai Phong International Container Terminal in the Lach Huyen port area. HHIT began operations in April 2025 and can accommodate container vessels with capacities of up to 18,000 TEUs. Hateco and APM Terminals are also pursuing cooperation on other port and logistics infrastructure projects in Vietnam. The wider planned investments involving Hateco and Maersk in Vietnam are estimated at between US$2.5 billion and US$3.5 billion. This amount does not represent the investment value of the railway freight terminal project alone.

articles.summary: AG Seville Shipyard has won the competition to continue operating the ship repair facilities at Spain’s Port of Seville, clearing an important hurdle for a proposed €10m ($11.2m) investment programme. Seville Port Authority’s board approved the selection of AG Seville Shipyard on October 20, allowing the company to...
articles.body: Uncategorized AG Seville wins 25-year port shipyard concession with $11m investment plan Splash Ports October 21, 2026 0 10 1 minute read AG Seville Shipyard AG Seville Shipyard AG Seville Shipyard has won the competition to continue operating the ship repair facilities at Spain’s Port of Seville, clearing an important hurdle for a proposed €10m ($11.2m) investment programme. Seville Port Authority’s board approved the selection of AG Seville Shipyard on October 20, allowing the company to retain its position at the former Astilleros del Guadalquivir facilities. The operator’s existing concession expires in December.The new concession will cover approximately 22,000 sq m of port land and infrastructure, including the dry dock, the southern section of the Muelle de Armamento and a disused slipway. The concession can run for up to 25 years, although final administrative approval is still required before the new agreement becomes effective. AG Seville Shipyard faced competition for the facilities from Spanish maritime group Boluda, which had also expressed interest in taking over the site. The successful operator has controlled part of the former Seville shipyard since 2017, developing ship repair and maintenance operations at facilities that had suffered years of decline following the collapse of the former public shipyard. The company plans to invest approximately €10m ($11.2m) in modernisation and expansion projects under the new concession. The tender conditions also require the successful operator to invest at least €3m ($3.4m) during the first three years, including improvements to the slipway and dry dock infrastructure. The larger €10m programme is AG Seville’s proposed investment plan, rather than an amount separately confirmed as contractually committed in the latest announcement. The port authority also approved an additional €4.2m ($4.7m) for improvements to Seville’s port free zone. The decision raises the total budget for modernising the area to €8m ($9m), covering electrical infrastructure, roads, lighting and other facilities serving businesses operating within the port’s industrial zone. The port authority will oversee procurement and technical management of the improvement projects. articles.body: Shipping leaders meet in Athens on 5 November 2026 SK Congress is organising the international maritime conference “Shipping at the Historic Turning Point of 2030” on 5 November 2026 at the InterContinental Athens, highlighting the major challenges, technological developments and strategic choices that will shape the future of global shipping. The conference is held under the auspices of the Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Insular Policy, the Ministry of Development, the Ministry of Digital Governance and Artificial Intelligence, the Ministry of Environment and Energy, the Region of Attica, the Hellenic Chamber of Shipping and the Athens Chamber of Commerce and Industry. The conference will be moderated by Nigel Lowry, Athens Correspondent of the international maritime newspaper Lloyd’s List, while journalist Giannis Moutsios will moderate the thematic panels. The discussions will focus, among other topics, on Artificial Intelligence and Automation, Alternative Fuels and Green Infrastructure, Geopolitical Challenges and Maritime Security, as well as the future of ports and shipyards. Particular emphasis will be placed on the leading role of Greek shipping and its prospects in a constantly changing international environment. The event aims to serve as a dynamic meeting point for shipowners, senior executives of shipping groups, institutional representatives, technology and energy companies, scientists, as well as representatives of ports, shipyards and international markets. SK Congress, which specialises in organising thematic, high-level maritime conferences, places particular emphasis on seamless organisation, attracting a carefully selected, high-quality audience, professional visibility and institutional prestige. Its goal is to create a platform for meaningful dialogue that will actively contribute to shaping the future of shipping. This will be followed by Closing Cocktail & Networking, with opportunities for meaningful networking, exchanging views and developing new professional partnerships. 2030: The new era of shipping starts now. articles.summary: SSE Renewables has named Seaway7 as the preferred supplier for the engineering, procurement, construction and installation (EPCI) of wind turbine...
articles.body: Cabling October 21, 2026 · 1 hour ago SSE taps Seaway7 for Scotland-bound inter-array cables, foundations 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Seaway Alfa Lift at Invergordon in northern Scotland; Source: SSE SSE Renewables has named Seaway7 as the preferred supplier for the engineering, procurement, construction and installation (EPCI) of wind turbine foundations and inter-array cables for its 1.4 GW Berwick Bank B offshore wind project in Scotland. The agreement, which covers the design, supply and installation of the foundations and subsea inter-array cables, remains subject to a final contract award, as SSE is targeting a final investment decision (FID) on Berwick Bank B in 2027. The planned work is expected to support 465 jobs across the UK, including 400 in Scotland, according to SSE. Seaway7 is expected to create around 160 direct roles, leading the work from its Aberdeen base, while another 105 jobs are anticipated in the UK supply chain. A further 200 direct and indirect jobs are expected through foundation marshalling at a Scottish port, to be announced later. SSE said the Seaway7 contract brings the number of jobs created or supported through its Berwick Bank B commitments to around 600 across the UK, including more than 500 in Scotland. These figures also include plans for an operations and maintenance base at Montrose Port, where 100 long-term jobs and around 30 construction roles are said to be created. Berwick Bank B is the second phase of SSE’s 4.1 GW Berwick Bank offshore wind project in the outer Firth of Forth, located around 38 kilometers off the Scottish Borders coast. The Scottish government granted consent for the full project in July 2025, and the 1.4 GW B phase secured a 20-year contract for difference (CfD) in the UK’s Allocation Round 7 in January 2026. The preferred supplier agreement between SSE and Seaway7 builds on the companies’ previous collaboration on the Beatrice and Seagreen offshore wind farms in Scotland, as well as their ongoing work on Dogger Bank in England, according to SSE. articles.title: Infill drilling ops underway offshore Oman with November start-up in sight
articles.summary: Masirah Oil has kicked off drilling of the first infill well at an oil field offshore Oman, with production expected as early as November 2026.
articles.body: Exploration & Production October 21, 2026 · 1 hour ago Infill drilling ops underway offshore Oman with November start-up in sight Masirah Oil has kicked off drilling of the first infill well at an oil field offshore Oman, with production expected as early as November 2026. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Block 50 lies in Gulf of Masirah, east of Oman Source: Masirah Oil Masirah Oil Limited (MOL), an indirect subsidiary of Singapore’s Rex International, has embarked on drilling operations at the first well of an offshore infill campaign in Block 50 off the coast of Oman, keeping the company on track for first oil in November 2026. Masirah Oil has announced that work on the first well in the infill campaign at the offshore Yumna field has commenced. Arabian Drilling signed a contract with Masirah Oil and Northern Offshore in August 2026 to drill two firm wells, in addition to two optional wells, in Oman. Mike Hopkinson , General Manager of Masirah Oil, commented: “We expect production from the new well to start in November 2026.” The Yumna field is situated in Block 50, which is an approximately 17,000 square-kilometer offshore concession located in the Gulf of Masirah, east of Oman. The first oil was achieved in February 2020. Rex’s subsidiary, MOL, an indirect 87.5% subsidiary of Jasmine Energy Limited (JEL), is the sole owner of the Block 50 concession. The Singaporean player holds an 87.5% interest in Masirah following restructuring. Block 50; Source: Masirah Oil The approval of the field development plan and declaration of commerciality (DOC) for the Yumna field were obtained in July 2020. Yumna-2 came online in January 2021, while Yumna-3 began production in February 2021. The following year, the floating storage tanker was changed out to allow for the tanker to be in the field for several years without the need for dry-docking. The mobile offshore production unit (MOPU) was also changed out with upgraded facilities the same year. The 4Q 2022 drilling campaign, which consisted of a workover of the Yumna-3 well to replace the electrical submersible pump and drilling of the Yumna-4 well that was completed for production, was finished in early 2023. MOL completed its multi-well program in 2024 at Block 50, including the drilling of the Yumna-5 well, which started production in April 2024, and workovers of three existing production wells, one more than originally planned. Masirah Oil emphasizes that the production rate is being regularly optimized to maximize recovery from the field, establish viable long-term production, and substantially increase the oil reserves at the block. articles.body: Oman’s Ministry of Transport, Communications and Information Technology has confirmed that a new operator will take over the Port of Salalah following the expiry of the existing concession agreement. Salalah Port Services Company SAOG will continue operating the port under the current concession until its contractual expiry on 1 November 2028. The company received formal notification that the agreement will not be extended beyond that date. The notification states that the decision not to extend the concession is final and unconditional. Operations to continue until concession expiry The Ministry said port operations and development activities will continue throughout the remaining concession period. The announcement forms part of the Ministry’s commitment to maintaining operational continuity while supporting the expansion and development of the Port of Salalah. The new operator that will assume responsibility for the port after the existing concession expires will be announced in due course. Company assesses implications Salalah Port Services said its Board of Directors will review the notification and assess its implications and potential impact on the company. The company will also engage with relevant stakeholders and provide the market with updates on any material developments in accordance with applicable disclosure requirements.

articles.title: Maersk eyes full return to Suez Canal by March 2027
articles.summary: Maersk expects all its shipping services to return to the Suez Canal by March 2027, according to the Suez Canal Authority (SCA), as the carrier continues to adjust its sailing schedules. The outlook was discussed during a video meeting between SCA Chairman Adm. Ossama Rabiee and senior Maersk executives, including...
articles.body: Maersk expects all its shipping services to return to the Suez Canal by March 2027, according to the Suez Canal Authority (SCA), as the carrier continues to adjust its sailing schedules. The outlook was discussed during a video meeting between SCA Chairman Adm. Ossama Rabiee and senior Maersk executives, including Chief Operating Officer Rabab Boulos. According to the SCA, Boulos expressed her expectation that all Maersk shipping services would resume transits through the canal by March next year. The timeline remains an expectation rather than a confirmed schedule for the full return of the carrier’s services. Maersk transits increase through Suez The Suez Canal Authority reported a significant increase in Maersk-affiliated vessel transits during the first nine months of 2026. Between January and September, 276 Maersk-affiliated vessels transited the canal, compared with 146 during the same period in 2025. This represents an increase of approximately 89%. The combined net tonnage of these transits reached 23.3 million tons, up from 7 million tons a year earlier. Rabiee highlighted the growing return of Maersk services and the importance of the canal for international shipping. He also pointed to the cost advantages of the Suez route compared with sailing around the Cape of Good Hope, particularly for large container vessels. Further service adjustments expected During the meeting, Ahmed Hassan, Vice President of Operations at Maersk, confirmed that the company continues to update its sailing schedules. These adjustments are expected to allow more Maersk services to transit the Suez Canal in the coming months. Hani El-Nady, Maersk’s representative in the Middle East and North Africa, also indicated that the group is working to accelerate the return of its services. However, the SCA announcement did not identify which additional services would return or provide specific dates for individual route changes. Both sides agreed to continue discussions on future cooperation as Maersk reviews its navigation plans.

articles.title: Australian fund takes control of UK ports giant in £10bn deal
articles.summary: Australian infrastructure investor IFM Investors has agreed to acquire a controlling stake in Associated British Ports (ABP), Britain’s largest port operator, in a deal valuing the business at more than £10bn ($13.4bn). The transaction will see Canadian pension giants CPP Investments and OMERS sell their combined...
articles.body: Europe Ports and Logistics Australian fund takes control of UK ports giant in £10bn deal Sam Chambers October 21, 2026 0 591 1 minute read Associated British Ports Associated British Ports Australian infrastructure investor IFM Investors has agreed to acquire a controlling stake in Associated British Ports (ABP), Britain’s largest port operator, in a deal valuing the business at more than £10bn ($13.4bn). The transaction will see Canadian pension giants CPP Investments and OMERS sell their combined 63.88% stake in ABP to Global Infraco Haven Bidco, an indirect subsidiary of the IFM Global Infrastructure Fund. ABP confirmed the binding agreement in a London Stock Exchange announcement today. Financial terms were not disclosed, although the Financial Times reported a valuation exceeding £10bn. The Australian group saw off competition from private equity heavyweights KKR and Apollo, as well as Indian billionaire Gautam Adani. ABP operates 21 ports across Britain, including Southampton, Immingham and the Humber complex, handling around a quarter of the country’s seaborne trade. Its activities span containers, vehicles, bulk commodities, cruise shipping and offshore energy infrastructure. The deal brings an end to two decades of Canadian involvement in the port operator. OMERS was part of the consortium that took ABP private in 2006 for £2.8bn, while CPP Investments acquired its interest in 2015. Singapore sovereign wealth fund GIC and Kuwait’s Wren House Infrastructure remain among the group’s minority investors. IFM is owned by Australian and British pension funds and manages around $96bn in infrastructure assets globally. The acquisition comes as ABP pursues substantial investment across its network. As Splash reported in August, the company is advancing a £500m development at Port Talbot in Wales to establish a major floating offshore wind manufacturing and assembly hub. Completion of the transaction remains subject to regulatory approvals and mandatory national security filings in the UK. articles.title: Norway set on tapping into Arctic gas potential: New study to unlock 1988 Barents Sea discovery
articles.summary: Norway is targeting untapped Arctic energy by commissioning a new study to shed more light on the 1988 gas discovery in the Barents Sea.
articles.body: Exploration & Production October 21, 2026 · 2 hours ago Norway set on tapping into Arctic gas potential: New study to unlock 1988 Barents Sea discovery Norway is targeting untapped Arctic energy by commissioning a new study to shed more light on the 1988 gas discovery in the Barents Sea. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 3 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Illustration Credit: Morten Berentsen/Norwegian Offshore Directorate Decades after being left behind in the frozen depths of the High North, a forgotten 1980s gas find in the Barents Sea is getting a second look. As Europe hungers for new energy sources and low-carbon reserves, Norway is launching a fresh push to unlock the untapped potential of the Arctic, starting with a neglected discovery 200 kilometers north of the Arctic Circle. The Barents Sea is home to a number of discoveries that could hold vast volumes of gas but remains less explored than other parts of the Norwegian Continental Shelf (NCS), with several discoveries in these waters potentially containing significant volumes of gas, according to the Norwegian Offshore Directorate, which emphasizes that a new study could uncover major opportunities for one of these discoveries. The gas discovery that this study will aim to gain more insight into is Norselhøgda (the well 7226/11-1 ), which is situated about 200 kilometers north of Hammerfest and was made in 1988. The discovery was production-tested, but the acreage was subsequently relinquished to the authorities. Arne Jacobsen , Assistant Director for Technology and Subsurface, commented: “Several major gas discoveries have been made in the Barents Sea which we still don’t know much about. Norselhøgda is one of a number of discoveries the Norwegian Offshore Directorate believes the companies should take a closer look at.” The Norwegian Offshore Directorate has hired the consulting company Terra Stream Energy to carry out a study that could bring new knowledge about the more precise volume of recoverable resources in the discovery. The reservoir is tight and will probably require stimulation . This is technology that is already being used on the NCS and elsewhere in the world. “The objective is to develop a model that can be shared with the companies so they can make further assessments of mapping and technologies that could help realize a potential development,” added Jacobsen. The study is scheduled to be completed towards the end of this year. In connection with this, the Norwegian Offshore Directorate plans to share the model and hold a professional seminar for the industry. Several comparable discoveries have been made in the area, which include production license 1313 , located to the north of the Norselhøgda discovery and awarded in APA 2025 . The Gro discovery in the Norwegian Sea is another discovery the Norwegian Offshore Directorate hopes to revive, along with the Linerle discovery in the Norwegian Sea. Related Articles Fossil Energy $1.42 trillion at stake as oil & gas production ebbs away: Norway urged to pick up the pace of exploration and tech advancement 3 min read “It’s possible that these discoveries could be viewed in an overall context. There could be benefits to extract if 1313 is developed further. The companies will have an opportunity to apply for Norselhøgda in the next APA round,” noted Jacobsen. The resource potential in the Barents Sea is considered to be considerable, as extensive parts of it remain largely unexplored, with significant acreage that has yet to be opened up for petroleum activity; thus, the development of this potential rests on the development of infrastructure and is particularly relevant for increased gas export opportunities. “Realizing Norselhøgda could be one step towards bringing this all into place,” underlined Jacobsen, while pointing out that the gas proven in the area has a very low CO2 content, just 0.3%, and development and production of gas with such low CO2 content provides added flexibility in exploiting existing infrastructure. articles.title: Equinor, SNOC to Explore Joint LPG Shipping, Storage and Trading in UAE
articles.summary: Norwegian energy company Equinor and Sharjah National Oil Corporation (SNOC) have signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) to explore cooperation in liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) and natural gas liquids (NGL) shipping, storage, trading and logistics in the United Arab Emirates.The agreement…
articles.body: Equinor, SNOC to Explore Joint LPG Shipping, Storage and Trading in UAE Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 21, 2026 (Credit: SNOC) Norwegian energy company Equinor and Sharjah National Oil Corporation (SNOC) have signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) to explore cooperation in liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) and natural gas liquids (NGL) shipping, storage, trading and logistics in the United Arab Emirates. The agreement, announced on October 20, establishes a framework for assessing potential business opportunities across the downstream oil and gas sector. The companies will evaluate cooperation in infrastructure, supply, shipping and trading of LPG, NGLs and other oil and gas products, alongside opportunities to optimise petrochemical storage facilities in the UAE. The MoU also covers selected energy transition opportunities, although the companies did not specify individual projects. The proposed cooperation would combine SNOC's existing infrastructure position with Equinor's equity volumes, trading capabilities, logistics operations and access to international markets. "By building a partnership around SNOC’s infrastructure position and Equinor’s equity volumes, trading, logistics and broad access to global markets, our two companies are positioned to create value-driven solutions to strengthen security of energy supply to regional and international markets," said Alex Grant, Equinor's Senior Vice President Crude, Products and Liquids Trading. "By combining our strengths, expertise and shared ambitions, we aim to enhance energy security, optimize infrastructure utilization and support the continued development of the UAE’s LPG sector. Most importantly, this collaboration will create long-term value for Sharjah, the UAE and the wider energy ecosystem," added Khamis Al Mazrouei, SNOC CEO. The companies plan to conduct a structured evaluation of potential commercial opportunities under the MoU. The agreement establishes a framework for cooperation rather than committing the companies to specific investments or projects.

articles.summary: Swedish ocean energy developer Minesto has been selected to participate in the Swedish government-backed initiative Sweden-Indonesia...
articles.body: Tidal & Wave Energy October 21, 2026 · 1 hour ago Minesto joins Swedish govt-backed initiative to work on tidal energy in Indonesia NS Nadja Skopljak Managing Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Minesto Swedish ocean energy developer Minesto has been selected to participate in the Swedish government-backed initiative Sweden-Indonesia Sustainability Partnership (SISP) to accelerate tidal energy development in Indonesia. SISP brings together Swedish companies and Indonesian stakeholders to accelerate the adoption of sustainable technologies and solutions. Within the partnership's Sustainable Energy Programme, Minesto will collaborate with Business Sweden to develop commercial opportunities for its tidal energy technology, including identifying strategic partners, facilitating access to financing and advancing project development. According to Minesto, Indonesia offers significant potential for tidal energy generation as its extensive network of islands and straits creates favorable conditions for harnessing tidal currents, with the country's total ocean energy potential estimated at approximately 60 GW. "Indonesia represents one of the largest global markets for our technology. The country's extensive tidal resources, combined with its growing demand for reliable renewable electricity, create significant opportunities. Being a part of the Sweden–Indonesia Sustainability Partnership strengthens our ability to turn this potential into commercial projects, working alongside Business Sweden and key Indonesian stakeholders," said Martin Edlund , CEO of Minesto. This builds on Minesto's ongoing business development in Indonesia. One of the opportunities is a tidal energy project at Nusa Penida, southeast of Bali, where Minesto is involved in feasibility assessments together with local partners. Through the collaboration with Business Sweden, Minesto said it would further strengthen local partnerships to advance project development. articles.title: Shipping equities turn geopolitical risk into an advantage
articles.summary: New research from investment bank Jefferies charts how shipping shares have shifted from being negatively correlated with geopolitical risk during the first decade of this century to moving increasingly in tandem with global instability since 2021. The new report is bullish on tankers, predicting that shares have...
articles.body: Containers Dry Cargo Gas Tankers Shipping equities turn geopolitical risk into an advantage Sam Chambers October 21, 2026 0 242 2 minutes read Photo by Aditya Vyas on Unsplash Photo by Aditya Vyas on Unsplash New research from investment bank Jefferies charts how shipping shares have shifted from being negatively correlated with geopolitical risk during the first decade of this century to moving increasingly in tandem with global instability since 2021. The new report is bullish on tankers, predicting that shares have further room to run, with rates forecast to taper more slowly than the market currently anticipates, in no small part down to the geopolitical correlation. “Since 2021, shipping stocks have also moved with our Geopolitical Risk Index every year, and we expect owners to keep capitalizing on the dislocation into 2027/2028+,” the report predicts. The underlying economics were neatly summarised by Navios Maritime Partners boss Angeliki Frangou during an August earnings call. “The longer ton-mile is like removing from the supply of vessels,” Frangou explained, pointing out that rerouting caused by the Red Sea and Hormuz crises meant ships were spending considerably longer at sea. Jan Rindbo, CEO of Norden, made a similar observation at last month’s Splash Singapore conference. “The world fleet is breaking down into smaller fleets,” Rindbo said, explaining how sanctions, regional conflicts and environmental regulations were fragmenting what was once a relatively unified global merchant fleet. The result is declining fleet efficiency, with more vessels required to transport the same quantities of cargo. Nikolas Tsakos, founder and CEO of Tsakos Energy Navigation, acknowledged the extraordinary opportunities created by the crisis during his company’s September earnings call. “This is uncharted territory, which we are taking advantage of carefully and steadily,” Tsakos said, while stressing his preference for peace even at the expense of today’s record returns. Jefferies believes the tanker rally has further to run, although not necessarily at today’s spectacular spot rates. The bank has lifted its 2027 VLCC earnings forecast from $60,000 to $65,000 a day and its LR2 projection from $30,000 to $34,000, arguing that persistent trading inefficiencies, ageing fleets and future oil inventory rebuilding will support earnings long after the current crisis subsides. It estimates that 51% of crude tankers are at least 15 years old, potentially helping absorb an orderbook equivalent to around 27% of the existing fleet. Not everyone shares that optimism. Norden’s Rindbo has warned that the tanker market could be approaching its peak, prompting the Danish group to reduce tanker exposure and redirect capital towards dry bulk. At Splash Singapore, Christoph Toepfer, CEO of Borealis Maritime, delivered an even starker warning. “The better the party, the worse is the hangover. We’re having a hell of a party right now,” he quipped. The question is how this extraordinary, record-breaking cycle ends. A remarkable chart from Clarksons Research, comparing today’s VLCC boom with previous peaks in capesizes, LNG carriers and container shipping, provides perspective. The current VLCC surge has reached around 17 times its long-term average, dwarfing the peaks recorded in earlier shipping cycles. Yet those previous booms eventually surrendered most of their extraordinary earnings premiums, often within just a few months. The VLCC line on the Clarksons chart ends at today’s extraordinary levels, leaving the subsequent trajectory unanswered. The industry’s history suggests that exceptional earnings eventually correct. What makes this cycle different is that nobody can confidently predict when the geopolitical distortions sustaining it will disappear, or how quickly an apparent shortage of tankers could turn into a surplus. articles.body: Europe Operations NATO boosts Black Sea surveillance amid attacks on shipping Adis Ajdin October 21, 2026 1 173 1 minute read NATO is deploying additional maritime patrol aircraft, drones and radar systems to the Black Sea following a series of deadly attacks on merchant shipping off Romania and Bulgaria. The move follows a meeting of the alliance’s North Atlantic Council in Brussels on Tuesday, with members also sending intelligence personnel and explosives investigation teams to the region. NATO military spokesman colonel Martin O’Donnell said the additional assets would strengthen surveillance and reconnaissance, with the emphasis on improving intelligence sharing and identifying threats to shipping. Bulgaria has already confirmed that a US Navy P-8 Poseidon maritime patrol aircraft has begun reconnaissance flights over the Black Sea following its request for assistance from NATO. Bulgarian prime minister Rumen Radev said allies had responded quickly to Sofia’s appeal, with further support expected. Four merchant ships have been attacked in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone over the past month, two of which sank. Allied specialists are also expected to help investigate the October 13 drone attack on the Malta-flagged general cargoship Chelsea 3 off Bulgaria. All 15 crewmembers were rescued, and investigators are examining recovered drone debris to establish the type of weapon used. The latest NATO response comes after a string of attacks on commercial vessels, including two chemical tankers off Romania last week. One of them, the Comoros-flagged Yara J , caught fire after a suspected drone strike inside Romanian territorial waters near the Sulina Canal. The crew managed to extinguish the blaze without outside assistance. The attacks have increasingly threatened shipping routes serving Ukraine’s Danube and Black Sea ports, adding to pressure on grain exports and pushing war-risk insurance costs higher. Russia’s defence ministry separately claimed on Tuesday that its forces had struck three cargo vessels at the Ukrainian port of Reni and another two heading towards Odesa, alleging that the ships were being used for military purposes. NATO has not formally attributed the recent attacks off Romania and Bulgaria to Russia, which has denied responsibility for those incidents. Despite the worsening security situation, Bulgarian authorities said commercial shipping to the Black Sea ports of Varna and Burgas was continuing, with no decline in vessel traffic reported. articles.title: Freightos Weekly Update: Red Sea container traffic set for full return in Q1
articles.summary: Trends in international ocean logistics seem even more confusing than usual lately: more Iranian attacks but more Hormuz traffic; more crude exports but oil prices still around $100 per barrel; more risk of Houthi attacks on passing ships, but more container vessels returning to the Red Sea anyway. Iran has stepped...
articles.body: Trends in international ocean logistics seem even more confusing than usual lately: more Iranian attacks but more Hormuz traffic; more crude exports but oil prices still around $100 per barrel; more risk of Houthi attacks on passing ships, but more container vessels returning to the Red Sea anyway. Iran has stepped up the frequency of attacks on vessels around the Strait of Hormuz, partially because transits and crude flows through the waterway have increased in recent weeks. Last week an Iranian projectile sunk a Dubai-linked container vessel, indicating that even some container ships are taking the risk of transiting the strait, though most traffic still comprises tankers. Despite some estimates that the increase in tankers exiting the Persian Gulf is contributing to Middle East crude exports approaching pre-war levels, crude prices – still pricing in elevated risk – remain high. Houthi-Saudi violence is intensifying, with recent Houthi advances along the Red Sea increasing its potential leverage over maritime traffic through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the likelihood of attacks on passing vessels. Despite that heightened risk – which since late 2023 had been enough to divert the vast majority of container traffic away from the Red Sea – container carriers continue their steady march back through the Suez, with estimates that transits will fully recover during Q1 of the coming year. Why carriers are more comfortable going back now than during similar, earlier high-risk stretches is a good question. The answer is probably a mix of high current fuel costs and congestion levels with evolving geopolitical considerations. These considerations may include, as Peter Tirschwell recently pointed out, Houthi interest in security and stability for most Red Sea traffic that could somewhat legitimize the group in relation to the West – alongside increased pressure directed at Saudi Arabia and its passing vessels. Whatever the reasons, that the Red Sea container rebound is happening gradually instead of all at once should mitigate the extent of schedule disruptions and vessel bunching that will occur as more vessels arrive earlier than slotted. That this restoration unfolded post the early-July Asia – Europe demand peak, and will continue through the coming low demand months will also mean less disruption to shippers than if the return coincided with peak season. Current port congestion levels – though backlogs and delays are finally easing at Far East hubs – continues to absorb some container capacity, and will help carriers maintain rate levels even as effective capacity increases from vessels circulating more quickly via the Red Sea. Overall though, the Red Sea return – if geopolitics allow its completion – increases the overcapacity risk for carriers in 2027. At the moment, even with Red Sea-driven effective capacity increases and slumping demand on Asia – Europe trades, spot rates are recently trending up on these lanes after months of declines. Asia – N. Europe Freightos Baltic Index rates climbed 6% last week to $3,442/FEU and prices to the Mediterranean increased 3% to $3,927/FEU on recent GRIs aimed at putting pressure on rates as 2027 long term contract negotiations get underway. Some forwarders are skeptical however, that increases will stick given current market conditions. Transpacific ocean rates were stable but still highly elevated last week at $8,126/FEU to the West Coast, with prices up 1% to $9,700/FEU for the East Coast. Daily rates so far this week are showing signs of increase – despite expectations that volumes are finally cooling – possibly due to capacity reductions as the lanes enter slow season. Last month some carriers announced plans for significanttransatlantic container price increases in October. So far though transatlantic spot rates have increased only about $200/FEU to $2,850/FEU since the end of September. Prices are however 25% higher than a year ago, possibly reflecting upward pressure from elevated bunker costs. In air cargo, the EU is set to introduce a November 1st €2 small parcel handling fee on top of the €3 customs surcharge introduced in July for low value imports that previously entered via the de minimis exemption. This additional fee could increase the China – Europe e-commerce volume draw down seen since July, which has led to some downward pressure on air cargo rates and shifted freighter capacity to other lanes. Freightos Air Index data show ex-China rates increased last week, possibly on a post-Golden Week backlog rebound or signalling the start of peak season pressure. Prices posted a sharp 19% gain to $6.88/kg to the US and an 8% climb to $3.87/kg to Europe. But while the global benchmark is 30% higher than a year ago on elevated fuel costs and volume growth – with transpacific rates 25% higher year on year – Asia – Europe prices are down 3% compared to last October, possibly reflecting e-commerce volume adjustments on this lane. articles.title: Iraqi Line returns to Gulf container trade after 50 years
articles.summary: Iraq’s national shipping line is returning to scheduled container services in the Gulf after more than half a century, as the country seeks to rebuild maritime connections disrupted by the Strait of Hormuz crisis. According to Alphaliner, Iraqi Maritime Line is deploying the 902 teu Basrah on an eight-day shuttle...
articles.body: Containers Middle East Iraqi Line returns to Gulf container trade after 50 years Sam Chambers October 21, 2026 0 733 1 minute read ICTSI ICTSI Iraq’s national shipping line is returning to scheduled container services in the Gulf after more than half a century, as the country seeks to rebuild maritime connections disrupted by the Strait of Hormuz crisis. According to Alphaliner, Iraqi Maritime Line is deploying the 902 teu Basrah on an eight-day shuttle linking Jebel Ali in Dubai with Umm Qasr, Iraq’s principal container gateway. The first sailing was scheduled to depart Jebel Ali yesterday, arriving in Umm Qasr two days later. Iraq’s transport ministry has described the initiative as the national carrier’s first regular Gulf operation since the mid-1960s. The relaunch comes as Iraqi container supply chains have been radically reshaped since the Hormuz shipping crisis erupted at the end of February. Growing volumes have been diverted to Jordan’s Red Sea port of Aqaba before travelling overland into Iraq through the Trebil border crossing. According to the Jordan Shipping Association, Aqaba handled 37,182 Iraq-bound transit containers during the first seven months of 2026, compared with just 3,599 during the corresponding period last year, a 933% increase. Maersk has introduced landbridge services connecting Aqaba with Iraq, while CMA CGM has offered alternative routings through Aqaba for southern Iraq and Turkey’s Mersin for northern destinations. The French carrier has also established multimodal connections through Saudi Arabia’s Jeddah and ports in Oman and the UAE. Other carriers have maintained limited maritime connections through smaller feeder vessels. Hapag-Lloyd outlined a routing in July whereby containers are discharged at Khorfakkan, outside the Strait of Hormuz, before being trucked across the UAE to Sharjah or Jebel Ali and transferred onto third-party feeder vessels serving Iraq and other upper Gulf destinations. The new Iraqi service will provide a dedicated national shipping connection with the region’s largest container hub, although vessels operating between Jebel Ali and Umm Qasr must still navigate the increasingly dangerous Strait of Hormuz. The shuttle therefore complements rather than replaces the overland alternatives that have become vital to keeping Iraqi imports moving. According to Xclusiv Shipbrokers, the New York-listed owner has lined up two ships at the CSSC-controlled yard, priced at around $109m each, with delivery scheduled for 2029. Neither Danaos nor the shipbuilder has publicly confirmed the deal. If finalised, it would mark the Greek owner’s first newbuilding contract at Waigaoqiao. Danaos has been a regular customer of Chinese shipyards in recent years, spreading orders across several builders as it renews and expands its containership fleet. The company already has seven 9,200 teu vessels under construction at other Chinese yards under contracts placed in 2024, with deliveries scheduled between 2027 and 2028. Its more recent investments include six 1,800 teu feeder vessels booked in November last year for delivery through 2029, followed by four 5,300 teu ships at CSSC Huangpu Wenchong, disclosed in February. Danaos’ latest corporate update, issued at the beginning of October, put its operating container fleet at 78 vessels totalling 502,265 teu, with another 28 newbuildings representing 177,776 teu of additional capacity. Beyond containers, Danaos has also been building a sizeable position in dry bulk. It owns 11 capesizes and has another four 211,000 dwt newcastlemaxes under construction at China’s Dajin Heavy Industry, representing an investment of about $297m. The group had been exploring a separate Oslo listing for its 15-ship bulker business, including a potential minority stake sale, as part of efforts to unlock value from the fleet. However, those plans have reportedly been put on hold after investor soundings failed to produce a satisfactory valuation amid weaker dry bulk freight rates and stock market conditions. Danaos has not formally confirmed the postponement or disclosed a revised timetable. The company had warned in its October 9 US securities filing that there was no guarantee the proposed listing would proceed. These include bunker-related surcharges, terminal handling charges at origin and destination, and safety and security charges. Other contingency and local charges may also apply. articles.title: North Sea gas field cleared for take-off: UK greenlights Jackdaw after legal storms
articles.summary: The UK regulator has given Shell-backed Adura the go-ahead for a North Sea gas field following a courtroom showdown with environmental campaigners.
articles.body: Authorities & Government October 21, 2026 · 4 hours ago North Sea gas field cleared for take-off: UK greenlights Jackdaw after legal storms The UK regulator has given Shell-backed Adura the go-ahead for a North Sea gas field following a courtroom showdown with environmental campaigners. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 4 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Jackdaw platform Source: Aker Solutions One of the North Sea’s most controversial gas projects has clawed its way back from the courtroom after climate legal challenges threw its future into limbo. Adura, an incorporated joint venture between UK-headquartered Shell and Norway’s Equinor, has now secured clearance to push ahead with Jackdaw, a high-stakes field designed to heat millions of British homes, even as environmental battles look set to rage on. The North Sea Transition Authority (NSTA) has granted development and production consent for the Jackdaw field off the coast of northeast Scotland to Adura, following the SoS’ consideration of the company’s environmental statement and agreement to the grant of consent. Stuart Payn , NSTA’s Chief Executive, commented: “After robust scrutiny we have today granted consent for the Jackdaw field development which allows the owners to proceed with their project and produce gas from the field upon completion of development work. “This project will support the UK’s energy security by providing domestically produced gas, generate tax revenues, safeguard supply chain jobs, use existing infrastructure, and have an emissions intensity well below the UK average.” Jackdaw has the potential to deliver around 6% of projected UK North Sea gas production, which is considered to be enough fuel to heat the equivalent of 1.4 million homes at a time when older gas fields are reaching the end of their production. Payn added: "Now is the time to move forward at pace and we welcome the government's approval in allowing us permission to consider a small number of new out of round licences ahead of forthcoming legislation." The field, located approximately 250 kilometers east of Aberdeen, is expected to be among the lowest-emission developments on the UK Continental Shelf (UKCS), while supporting jobs and bolstering Britain’s energy security. Previously, the NSTA gave consent on June 1, 2022, to develop the Jackdaw project after the Offshore Petroleum Regulator for Environment & Decommissioning (OPRED) agreed to the grant of consent for the development following an assessment of the environmental impacts of the project. However, Greenpeace asked the Scottish Court to review the grant of consent and OPRED’s agreement to the grant of consent in relation to the planning application and the need to consider not only the emissions from the platform’s operations but also the emissions when the gas is used by customers. The UK Supreme Court issued a judgment in a case referred to as ‘Finch’ in 2024 , regarding a proposed oil well in Surrey that was approved by the local council in 2019, ruling that the approval should also have considered the emissions produced by the oil’s end use as well as those emissions caused by the oil well’s operations. Afterward, the Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled on January 30, 2025, that the previous government’s decision to approve the Jackdaw and Rosebank oil fields was unlawful. As a result, the court overturned the decision, accepting Uplift’s argument that the government failed to consider the emissions that would be caused by burning the oil and gas produced by these fields when it approved them. Related Articles Fossil Energy Multi-billion projects at stake: Another blow for UK’s largest untapped oil & gas duo but Shell, Equinor, and Ithaca remain upbeat 14 min read Adura has continued to comply with all laws and regulations relating to the Jackdaw project situated in blocks 30/02a, 30/03a, and 30/02d of the United Kingdom Continental Shelf that lies in a water depth of approximately 78 meters. The field is located in the Central North Sea (CNS), 30 kilometers southeast of the Shearwater platform and adjacent to the UK/Norway median line. Jackdaw is a gas/condensate development comprising a not permanently attended wellhead platform with four wells, tied back to the Shearwater hub via a 31-kilometer pipeline. The steel jacket and topside were installed in August 2023 and October 2025, respectively. The pipeline was laid in July 2024 and the drilling activities were completed in early 2026. While the latest approval marks a major turning point, the environmental battles are not entirely over since environmental groups like Greenpeace remain strongly opposed to the development of the North Sea oil and gas projects, which have become a primary battleground for climate litigation. As a result, activists continue to scrutinize these approvals. By resubmitting the required environmental statements and clearing this regulatory hurdle, the Jackdaw project has overcome the specific legal blockades that previously stalled it, allowing developers to finally move forward even if political and activist friction persists. Responding to the government giving the Jackdaw gas field the go-ahead, Sam Richards , CEO of Britain Remade, said: “Britain is going to need gas for decades to come, as even the Climate Change Committee recognises. The choice is not between gas and no gas, but between gas produced in British waters and gas shipped in from abroad at higher cost and with higher emissions. “But while we should use what we have, the North Sea is a declining basin, and we need to transition to homegrown clean power. Britain’s always-on electricity should come from new clean nuclear, both gigawatt-scale reactors and small modular reactors that can be sited in far more places than their bigger cousins. “Right now Britain is the most expensive place in the world to build new nuclear. articles.title: The empty container problem isn’t a shortage. It’s a data problem.
articles.summary: Container shipping has just lived through its third consecutive year of a peak season that arrived early and left just as fast. Shippers rushed cargo out ahead of the July 1 bunker adjustment factor reset, itself a product of fuel costs pushed up by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Meanwhile, continued avoidance...
articles.body: Container shipping has just lived through its third consecutive year of a peak season that arrived early and left just as fast. Shippers rushed cargo out ahead of the July 1 bunker adjustment factor reset , itself a product of fuel costs pushed up by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Meanwhile, continued avoidance of the Red Sea cut effective fleet capacity by around 12%, with slow steaming absorbing another 2%, according to MPC Container Ships chief executive Constantin Baack. Idle capacity opened 2026 at just 0.6% of the global fleet. When ships run this close to full utilization, there’s no cushion left for the equipment side, either. A terminal that’s short on boxes during a front-loading rush can be sitting on a surplus a few weeks later, paying storage and demurrage on equipment nobody is ready to move. Imbalances like this are nothing new. They’re just happening more often and swinging harder, leaving less room to manage equipment by gut feel. The boxes stacking up in a yard are the part everyone can see, but they’re the symptom of a second pile that gets far less attention: the data sitting unused in the systems that were supposed to prevent this in the first place. The second pile Carriers, lessors, depots and container-heavy shippers aren’t short on information. TMS records, telematics feeds, gate moves, EDI booking data, depot inventories – most companies already have all of it. The trouble is that it lives in separate systems, owned by separate teams, built to answer separate questions. Ask a planner where the network will be short in six weeks and where it’ll be long, and by the time anyone assembles an answer, the window to do anything useful with it has usually closed. That’s how a network ends up with shortages and surpluses side by side; a carrier leasing boxes at a premium at one port while, three time zones away, a terminal pays to store idle ones. Sometimes, both locations sit on the same trade lane, run by the same planning team, looking at data that was never merged. That disconnect costs money and undermines sustainability, standardization, safety, and security. The fix for each one, however, starts in the same place. In practice, the data gap shows up in four places: sustainability, standardization, safety, and security. Sustainability: fewer empty miles Moving empty boxes around has always been part of the business. But Sea-Intelligence calculated this year that repositioning empties now accounts for 30% of all container shipping work measured in TEU-miles, up from 24% before the 2020 pandemic. The number of empty containers shipped has grown 65% since early 2019, while full containers grew 17%. Each empty leg takes up a vessel slot and a crane lift, often with a truck or train move at either end, and it burns fuel without earning a cent. In June, Hapag-Lloyd told customers that operational disruptions were costing $50 million to $60 million a week, and the carrier has pointed to storage and inland transport as part of that bill. A lot of empty moves exist to clean up earlier planning: a box gets sent somewhere on the assumption it’ll be needed, demand shifts, and a few weeks later it’s on the move again. The way out is to plan empty flows ahead of time instead of reacting once the imbalance is obvious. A twelve- to sixteen-week forecast gives planners enough runway to reposition before a shortage hits, and also allows them to weigh the cost of storing a box against moving it across the whole network. If holding a container at a secondary depot is cheaper, that should be settled once, not argued over every week by whoever happens to be on shift. Every reactive move that doesn’t happen saves fuel and emissions, and often a storage or demurrage charge as well. Getting there doesn’t take a single new ship or container. Standardization starts with the inputs A forecast can only work with data that lines up. Containers have a head start here that most industries would envy: every box carries an identity that means the same thing everywhere, thanks to an owner code register BIC has published continuously since 1970. Location codes follow UN/LOCODE, and the Digital Container Shipping Association (DCSA), whose members account for about 75% of global container trade, has published data standards for bookings, track and trace and more. Implementation is where it falls down: early rollouts varied so much that, since mid-2025, the DCSA only lists the ones that pass its conformance testing. Regulation is pushing in the same direction. Since January 1, 2026, amendments to SOLAS require every container lost or seen drifting at sea to be reported, and flag states now have to send annual loss figures to the International Maritime Organization (IMO). Until now, the industry relied on voluntary surveys to count losses, which the World Shipping Council estimates reached 1,478 containers in 2025. A mandatory, common reporting format is standardization at its most basic level. For equipment planning, the day-to-day version of this is smaller and, quite frankly, more irritating. Two terminals on the same lane log a gate-out slightly differently, or a partner’s EDI feed codes a 40-foot high cube one way while the depot system codes it another, and suddenly the numbers don’t add up. Before a forecast is worth trusting, booking patterns, gate moves, depot stock, and seasonal demand have to be pulled together and organized consistently by container type and location. Nobody needs to collect anything new to do that. Safety: getting unsafe boxes out of circulation in time Most planners know where their containers are, but far fewer know what state those containers are in; inspection and repair records usually live in maintenance systems the planning desk never opens. Under the Convention for Safe Containers, every box has to be examined on a fixed schedule or under an approved continuous examination programme, and a container damaged badly enough to be unsafe has to come out of service. The approved programmes themselves are published in the Global ACEP Database, which BIC runs on the IMO’s recommendation. The trouble starts when the exam schedule and the repositioning plan sit in separate systems: that’s how a container a few weeks from its exam date ends up on a long loop, or a damaged unit stays in use because the depot where it landed had no repair slot planned. Condition also means cleanliness. The International Plant Protection Convention’s recommendation on the sea container pathway names incomplete unpacking and cleaning as a main source of pest contamination, and calls for empty containers to be examined and cleaned. Empties are exactly the boxes a repositioning plan moves around, so the same forecast that decides where they go can decide when they get checked. Once condition data is part of the forecast, a planner can book repairs at the depots where boxes are going to sit idle anyway, and send units due for inspection or cleaning toward a facility that can handle them. Deciding whether to repair or retire a box then happens on a schedule rather than in a rush. Security: knowing what should be where Gaps between systems are also where criminals do their best work. Just last year, the World Customs Organization analyzed more than 2,600 drug seizures, and found that 68% involved someone working inside the maritime cargo supply chain. Containers accounted for 85% of the seizure events. One finding should worry anyone managing empty equipment: gangs are increasingly hiding smaller loads inside the structure of refrigerated containers and collecting them at unsecured empty container yards once customs has cleared the box, often with help from insiders who can see logistics systems. A network that forecasts where every box should be over the coming weeks has a baseline to check against, and a container sitting somewhere no booking explains – or one that has gone quiet for longer than usual – shows up as an exception instead of going unnoticed in an export file. That same record of equipment moves is also what compliance teams need when sanctions or conflict force a route change. An intelligent layer, not another system Most operators have invested heavily in the systems they run, and they’re right to be wary of anyone telling them to start over. But they don’t need to; the data for all of this already exists. What’s missing is something that reads systems together and turns data into a forecast planners can act on weeks ahead. Ideally, it stays in the background, flagging when two terminals’ records don’t match, when a box due for inspection is about to head the wrong way, or when an empty in one yard is what another port will be short of next month. Veson Nautical in July put the container orderbook at close to 40% of the existing fleet, with growth expected to outpace demand through the end of the decade. The next swing will hit a network with almost no idle capacity to absorb it, and the operators that handle it best will be the ones making full use of what they know about the boxes they have. For them, better forecasting means fewer empty miles, data that lines up across partners, unsafe boxes pulled before they cause harm, and fewer blind spots for criminals to exploit – covering all four S’s with information they already hold. The corridor’s structure Russian gate, Chinese operators, energy cargo did not change. This content is locked Select a CN Premium Subscription Package To Unlock The Content! Register By the end of September, the Northern Sea Route had logged 104 confirmed transit voyages, already above the 103 recorded across the whole of 2025. Transit cargo reached an estimated 3.7 million tonnes, 15% more than last year, and the Centre for High North Logistics expects the season to approach 150 transits and 4.5 million tonnes. The numbers confirm momentum but not transformation: the season grew along lines the corridor’s structure already permitted. Twenty-two eastbound tanker voyages carried about 2.1 million tonnes, mostly crude loaded at Murmansk, Primorsk and Ust-Luga. That is Baltic oil leaving a sea where boardings, inspections and drone strikes have raised enforcement risk, and travelling east through waters Russia administers alone. Bulk carriers added 1.1 million tonnes, while 27 westbound bulk voyages repositioned tonnage toward the Baltic. Crude and bulk together account for roughly 86% of transit cargo. The NSR remains an energy and bulk artery, not a substitute for Suez. Nor has the gate moved. Rosatom issued every permit for the season and manages the route in 28 sections; each newcomer, from South Korea’s Panstar Acro to the Chinese container operators, entered by Russian approval. External pull is stronger than the series’ base case assumed, with the Gulf war disrupting southern energy flows, but that pull feeds a corridor whose access terms Moscow alone sets. Weather also helped: favourable late-season ice postponed, rather than removed, the ceiling that icebreaker capacity and short navigation windows impose. Containers are where the season broke new ground. Sea Legend completed all eight weekly sailings of its China–Europe Arctic Express, moving more than 14,000 TEU of export cargo on seven ice-strengthened ships. International Asia–Europe container transits rose from one in 2025 to four by end-September, with vessels reaching the United Kingdom from Korea and China. After demonstration voyages in 2023–24 and trials in 2025, 2026 produced the first seasonal liner product: fixed departures, dedicated tonnage and a published transit time. “The split runs through carriers and capital, not through cargo and ports.” The product’s character matters more than its novelty. It is Chinese-operated, seasonal, small-ship the largest vessel carries 4,890 TEU and driven by westbound exports. Its entire season moved less than one ultra-large container ship carries on a single voyage. It competes with rail and air-sea for time-sensitive peak-season cargo, not with Suez mainline services. And it leaves Western carriers absent without excluding Western economies: no European or American line runs a comparable service, yet the boxes land at Felixstowe and other Western ports. The next stage points to density rather than scale. NewNew Shipping targets 1.2 million tonnes for 2027 with two sailings a month and has signalled interest in investing in Russian Arctic ports, while Murmansk is building a partnership with it. That would extend Chinese institutionalisation into Russian physical infrastructure and deepen the lock-in that keeps Western carriers out. The binding constraints remain: Sea Legend ended departures early on ice forecasts even in a favourable year, and the service relies on repurposed, ageing tonnage rather than purpose-built ice-class ships. The likely outcome is a durable Chinese seasonal niche commercially marginal, strategically significant, and operating at Russia’s discretion.

That followed the July sale of another 2007-built VLGC, BW Elm , which generated around $64m in cash and a $36m book gain. Including BW Loyalty, the three announced transactions represent approximately $194m in net cash proceeds and $125m in gains on a 100% basis, although the latest sale has yet to close. The disposals come as BW LPG embarks on its largest newbuilding programme in years. In May, the company contracted eight 90,000 cu m panamax VLGCs at HD Hyundai Heavy Industries for approximately $940m, with deliveries scheduled between 2029 and 2030. articles.title: Project Cargo East of Suez: Routing Oversized Freight When the Short Way Is Not Simple
articles.summary: Since late 2023, attacks on merchant shipping around the southern Red Sea have changed how many carriers route between Asia, the Red Sea, the Gulf and East Africa. Much of the public discussion has focused on standard containers and headline freight rates. For shippers of project and oversized cargo, such as...
articles.body: Since late 2023, attacks on merchant shipping around the southern Red Sea have changed how many carriers route between Asia, the Red Sea, the Gulf and East Africa. Much of the public discussion has focused on standard containers and headline freight rates. For shippers of project and oversized cargo, such as machinery, generators, steel structures and plant modules, the change has been more awkward. Their cargo depends on special equipment, careful planning and fewer options. This piece does not try to predict when conditions will change. It sets out the practical questions we now work through on every out-of-gauge file headed to these regions. Suez or the Cape: a decision made shipment by shipment For cargo moving between Asia and Europe or the Mediterranean, many carriers have chosen the Cape of Good Hope over the Suez Canal. That adds sailing time and changes port rotations. For cargo whose destination is itself on the Red Sea, such as Jeddah, Port Sudan, Aqaba or Hodeidah, sailing around the Cape is not the answer. The question becomes which carriers still call, how they call, and through which hub. This means routing decisions are made shipment by shipment rather than lane by lane. A routing that worked last quarter may not be offered now, and the same carrier may treat different destination ports differently. For oversized cargo, which often has a fixed site date and limited equipment, a quote should state the actual routing and carrier. A generic transit time is not enough. Hub switching and the extra handling it brings When direct calls are withdrawn, cargo is often moved through a transhipment hub and then a feeder or regional service. For standard boxes, that mostly means extra time. For project cargo, every extra lift is a risk. A flat rack carrying an over-width unit must be handled, stowed and lashed correctly at each terminal. Not every hub or feeder vessel is equally suited to out-of-gauge units. Before booking, we ask three things. Will the hub accept the unit’s dimensions and weight? Can the connecting vessel stow it on or under deck as needed? How long is the unit likely to wait for a connection? A switch of hub after booking can mean a new acceptance process, so it pays to confirm acceptance with the carrier for the full routing, not only the first leg. Flat racks and open tops: equipment is part of the plan Special equipment is not evenly distributed. Flat racks and open-top containers have to be positioned where the cargo is. When services change, empty special equipment can end up in the wrong place. Shippers should ask early whether the required equipment is available at the loading port for the intended sailing, and plan production around it. When out-of-gauge acceptance on container services is limited, breakbulk or a combination of containers and breakbulk becomes a real option. For some units, conventional vessels or multipurpose ships offer a more direct route to the destination than a container network that has been redesigned around the disruption. The right answer depends on dimensions, weight, destination port facilities and timing. War-risk insurance and surcharges Carriers may apply war-risk or emergency surcharges on affected lanes, and marine insurers may apply additional premiums for voyages through listed areas. These can change at short notice. Shippers should check three things. Does the freight quote include or exclude these surcharges? Does the cargo insurance policy cover the actual routing, including any listed areas? Who under the agreed Incoterm bears the cost if surcharges are introduced after booking? Agreeing this clearly in the sales contract avoids disputes later. Documents: small errors, large delays Rerouting and transhipment add places where documents can cause trouble. Bills of lading must reflect the actual port of discharge and any agreed place of delivery. For project cargo, packing lists should give accurate dimensions and weights for every piece, together with lifting points and centre-of-gravity details where relevant. Several destinations in the Red Sea, Gulf and East Africa have their own import documentation, pre-shipment certification or registration requirements. These should be confirmed with the consignee and destination agent before the cargo leaves origin, not after it arrives. What shippers can do now The common thread is to plan earlier and in more detail. In practice, that means: – Get routing and carrier details in writing for the specific destination port. – Confirm out-of-gauge acceptance for every leg, including the hub. – Check special equipment availability before fixing production dates. – Compare container and breakbulk options for oversized units. – Clarify war-risk surcharges and insurance cover against the actual routing. -Confirm destination document requirements before shipment. Conditions on these lanes may continue to shift, and I will not try to say how or when. What does not change is that project cargo rewards careful preparation. Shippers who ask these questions early keep more options open when routings move. About the author Delia Qu is Deputy General Manager at Dalian Yihang Shipping Agency Co., Ltd., a Class-1 international freight forwarder, NVOCC and AEO Advanced Certified customs broker in Dalian, China. She has more than ten years of experience in freight forwarding. Founded in 2020, the company handles ocean FCL and LCL, air freight, China–Europe rail, project and breakbulk cargo, and exhibition cargo to more than 80 countries through 180+ overseas agents.

articles.title: HarborLab: Why shipping’s husbandry bills are still stuck in Excel
articles.summary: Shipping has spent years tightening voyage costs, bunker procurement and commercial port expenses, but one sizeable part of the bill remains comparatively untouched: husbandry. articles.body: Europe Maritime CEO Operations Tech HarborLab: Why shipping’s husbandry bills are still stuck in Excel Splash October 21, 2026 0 319 3 minutes read HarborLab HarborLab Shipping has spent years tightening voyage costs, bunker procurement and commercial port expenses, but one sizeable part of the bill remains comparatively untouched: husbandry. For Antonis Malaxianakis, founder and CEO of Athens-based port cost management platform HarborLab, that blind spot is particularly evident around bunkering, crew changes and stores, where technical departments can still be managing substantial sums through spreadsheets and email. “Husbandry calls have never carried the same profit and loss visibility as commercial port calls,” Malaxianakis tells Maritime CEO. The absence of cargo revenue against which expenditure can be measured has meant these calls have escaped some of the scrutiny applied elsewhere in ship operations. At the same time, the invoices are anything but simple. A port call can generate hundreds of pages involving port authorities, pilots, tug operators, customs brokers, bunker suppliers, repair companies and other parties. Pricing may vary even within the same port, while additional items such as demurrage, detention, congestion surcharges and equipment rental can emerge later. For Malaxianakis, who worked in disbursement departments at Thenamaris and Product Shipping & Trading before founding HarborLab in 2020, the problem is less about a lack of attention from technical managers than the tools available to them. The gap is particularly pronounced in Asia. “One data point from our analysis makes the structural difference concrete: 75% of technical managers in APAC still manage husbandry bills in Excel today, compared with 40% in EMEA,” he says. Across much of Asia, technical managers have direct control over dayto-day port expenditure but often lack a live reference against which an agent’s quote can be checked. HarborLab sees that combination as one reason APAC has become a priority market. “That combination, direct spending authority paired with heavier reliance on manual tools, does leave APAC more exposed to inconsistent pricing,” Malaxianakis explains.“The decision-maker already controls the budget; they’re simply working without the visibility to know whether what’s being paid is fair.” HarborLab argues that the difference between checking whether an invoice matches a quoted tariff and determining whether the quoted price was reasonable in the first place is where much of the potential saving sits. The company points to a controlled three-month trial with one customer in which half of a fleet remained on its existing disbursement account process while the other half moved to HarborLab. The HarborLab-managed vessels generated $220,000 in savings compared with $70,000 on the other half. “The gap isn’t down to one single lever, but the largest multiplier is benchmarking,” Malaxianakis says. “Manual review, however careful, can only check an invoice against a tariff document or a prior year’s DA; it can confirm a charge matches what was quoted, not whether the quote itself was fair.” HarborLab checks individual expense items against its database covering more than 1,400 ports. The system also picks up incorrect and duplicated charges, with the company then taking discrepancies back to agents in an effort to turn the finding into a credit. Benchmarking port calls is not as straightforward as comparing a bunker price or a standard commodity rate, however. Local tariffs, vessel types and individual port requirements mean two apparently similar services can legitimately carry very different costs. Malaxianakis argues that broad averages would therefore create another problem rather than solve the existing one. “Every benchmark is built at the level of port, vessel type, and expense category, not as one blended number, so a crane charge on an MR tanker at Tarragona is a different data point from the same charge on a bulker at Rotterdam,” he says. Behind that sits a database built from more than 40,000 port calls across over 1,400 ports. HarborLab says its analysts also obtain and verify official tariffs directly with ports rather than relying solely on historical invoices. Comparisons are then made against previously approved disbursement accounts for comparable ports and vessel types, while tariffs carry confidence indicators showing technical managers whether the underlying figure has been independently verified. “Local variation is built into the comparison rather than smoothed over,” Malaxianakis says. For a sector increasingly comfortable using data to scrutinise fuel consumption, vessel performance and voyage economics, his argument is that the same level of attention has yet to reach every invoice arriving from shore. And in husbandry, there is still plenty sitting in the spreadsheet. articles.body: Offshore Woodside resumes Scarborough work after Greenpeace protest Bojan Lepic October 21, 2026 0 63 1 minute read Greenpeace Greenpeace Australian energy major Woodside has resumed commissioning at its Scarborough gas project offshore Western Australia after Greenpeace activists occupied the site over the weekend, forcing a temporary suspension of work. The company confirmed operations restarted after the remaining protesters were removed from the 70,000-tonne floating production unit, located about 375 km off the Pilbara coast. Four Greenpeace activists boarded the facility on Saturday after arriving aboard the Rainbow Warrior , unfurling a banner calling for an end to Woodside’s gas developments near Scott Reef. Two activists remained overnight in suspended tents before being removed by police helicopter on Sunday. Woodside described the unauthorised access as “dangerous, reckless and illegal”, warning that the incident had triggered a potentially costly response. The occupation suspended pre-commissioning activities. The environmental group claims Woodside plans to drill up to 57 wells around the reef, threatening marine habitats, including endangered pygmy blue whales and nesting green sea turtles. Two men, aged 48 and 52, were subsequently charged with interfering with offshore petroleum installations or operations, an offence carrying a maximum prison sentence of 10 years. Greenpeace continued its campaign, delivering a 47-metre-long petition bearing nearly half a million signatures to Woodside’s headquarters in Perth. The disruption comes as Woodside moves towards the first LNG shipment from its $12.5bn Scarborough development. In its latest quarterly update, Woodside said the project was 99% complete at the end of September, with gas already introduced into the offshore production unit and export pipeline. The company maintained that Scarborough remains on budget and on track to deliver its first LNG cargo in the fourth quarter of 2026.
