U.S. Coast Guard Photo The U.S. Coast Guard Cutter Munro has returned to its homeport in Alameda, California, following a 112-day patrol across the Bering Sea and Arctic Ocean that included monitoring Chinese research vessels, conducting joint exercises with Canadian forces and enforcing U.S. fisheries laws. The 418-foot national security cutter covered more than 23,000 nautical miles during the deployment, part of a broader effort to maintain a U.S. presence in the Arctic as Chinese and Russian activity draws increasing attention from Washington. Operating under the Coast Guard Arctic District, Munro monitored three Chinese-flagged research vessels operating in and around U.S. Arctic waters under Operation Frontier Sentinel, an ongoing effort to track foreign activity near Alaska and protect U.S. sovereign rights. The patrol included the July monitoring of the Chinese research ships Xue Long and Xue Long 2 , which transited north through the U.S. Exclusive Economic Zone and over the U.S. extended continental shelf in the Bering Sea. Foreign vessels are permitted to transit these waters under international law, but conducting marine scientific research within the U.S. EEZ or on its extended continental shelf requires prior U.S. authorization. The Coast Guard has said its monitoring operations are intended to ensure compliance with those rules and allow a rapid response to potentially unauthorized activity. The Coast Guard did not identify the third Chinese vessel monitored during the deployment in its latest announcement. Munro also conducted joint exercises with the Royal Canadian Navy, focusing on maritime law enforcement cooperation, maneuvering and improving awareness of vessel activity in Arctic waters. The cutter additionally participated in Operation Tundra Merlin, which brought together U.S. and Canadian military assets to test communications, command-and-control systems and coordinated responses to potential threats in northern maritime approaches. “The Arctic is a demanding maritime environment that can test any crew and vessel,” said Capt. Adam J. Disque, Munro ‘s commanding officer. “We also strengthened our enduring partnership with Canadian counterparts, advancing shared domain awareness and coordination across the remote region,” he added. Beyond its security mission, Munro conducted fisheries enforcement patrols in the Bering Sea, where boarding teams inspected commercial fishing vessels for compliance with federal safety regulations and fisheries laws. The Coast Guard described the mission as protecting Alaska’s commercial fishing industry, valued at approximately $6 billion. The deployment comes as the Coast Guard faces growing demands in the Arctic while operating with a limited number of ice-capable vessels. In September, the service confirmed to gCaptain that the medium icebreaker Healy would not complete its planned 2026 high-latitude mission following a significant engineering casualty in July. The breakdown left the Coast Guard relying more heavily on other assets, including the recently commissioned icebreaker Storis , national security cutters and aircraft, to maintain surveillance and patrol operations across the region. China’s growing Arctic presence has become a particular focus. Chinese research ships have conducted increasingly visible operations in northern waters, prompting U.S. and Canadian authorities to expand monitoring of their activities. The Coast Guard has emphasized that the presence of foreign research vessels is not itself a violation of international law, but says continued monitoring is necessary to protect U.S. interests in the region. Commissioned in 2017, Munro is one of four Legend-class national security cutters homeported in Alameda. The ship returned to Coast Guard Island on Friday following its nearly four-month deployment. articles.summary: The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers is overhauling how it manages dredging contracts nationwide, moving toward a centralized approach intended to reduce costs, improve scheduling and make better use of...

Stock Photo: Daniel Wright98/Shutterstock The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers is overhauling how it manages dredging contracts nationwide, moving toward a centralized approach intended to reduce costs, improve scheduling and make better use of the country’s limited dredging fleet. The Corps handles approximately 190 dredging contract actions each year to maintain navigation channels at U.S. ports, harbors and inland waterways. Most have traditionally been managed by individual districts, an approach the agency says can lead to duplicated administrative work, competing schedules and inefficient use of available dredging equipment. To address those problems, the Corps is establishing an Enterprise Dredging Delivery Center (EDDC), supported by an interim Dredging Evolution for Enterprise Production (DEEP) Team, to coordinate dredging requirements across the country. The goal is to treat dredging as a national program rather than a series of largely independent projects, allowing the Corps to coordinate contracts, schedules and equipment needs across multiple waterways. “For decades, we have approached dredging as a collection of individual projects—one district develops a contract, one gets awarded, and one dredge gets mobilized,” said Maj. Gen. Jason E. Kelly, while serving as the Corps’ deputy commanding general for civil and emergency operations. “While that model built today’s system, it is insufficient for the challenges we face tomorrow. The American taxpayer is not paying us to award contracts; they are paying us to maintain navigation channels.” Under the new approach, individual Corps districts will continue identifying dredging needs, handling engineering and environmental requirements, and coordinating with local ports and stakeholders. The centralized delivery center will provide contracting and planning support, with an emphasis on coordinating projects that compete for the same equipment and contractors. The changes could have significant implications for the U.S. dredging industry, where vessel availability, mobilization costs and project timing play major roles in determining how much work can be completed. By providing contractors with greater visibility into upcoming projects, the Corps hopes to reduce scheduling conflicts and give companies more certainty when planning vessel deployments, staffing and equipment investments. The agency has already begun testing new contracting approaches. In September, the Corps outlined plans to consolidate portions of its dredging workload into larger contracts and develop national procurement strategies. One initiative, called “Scope Dredge to Budget,” would allow contractors to compete on how much dredging they can accomplish within a predetermined budget, rather than simply bidding on a fixed quantity of material. The Corps held an industry meeting on October 16 to discuss applying the approach to navigation channels in Texas, including the Houston Ship Channel, Sabine-Neches Waterway and Corpus Christi Ship Channel. The broader restructuring is being introduced in phases, with the Corps previously identifying October 2027 as its target for establishing the permanent delivery center. The agency says it will continue consulting with dredging contractors and port stakeholders as the program develops, particularly to ensure that larger procurement packages do not undermine competition or disadvantage smaller and specialized operators. The initiative is part of the Army’s broader “Building Infrastructure, Not Paperwork” effort, which seeks to reduce administrative requirements and direct more resources toward infrastructure improvements. For the Corps, the ultimate measure of success will be whether the changes translate into more dredging and more reliable access to the nation’s ports and waterways. “The measure of success is not how many contracts we award; it is how many cubic yards we move,” Kelly said. “It is whether America’s navigation system is ready when the nation needs it.” Sign up for gCaptain’s newsletter and never miss an update Essential maritime and offshore news, insights, and updates delivered daily straight to your inbox Dive into a sea of curated content with our weekly ‘Dispatch’ email. "The conversation around AI and robotics in defense is no longer about experimental technology. It's about delivering measurable and impactful returns," said Jake Loosararian, Gecko Robotics co-founder and CEO. articles.summary: Iran’s Revolutionary Guards claimed Tuesday that a supertanker caught fire after striking a naval mine south of the Strait of Hormuz, adding to a series of similar claims that have...

REUTERS/Stringer Iran’s Revolutionary Guards claimed Tuesday that a supertanker caught fire after striking a naval mine south of the Strait of Hormuz, adding to a series of similar claims that have yet to be independently substantiated. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said the tanker was violating Iranian transit regulations when it struck a mine, according to Reuters. In another statement carried by Iranian media Tuesday , the Guards said two tankers had been set ablaze and disabled by mines along a route south of the strait that Tehran considers unauthorized. Neither statement identified the vessels or provided independently verifiable evidence of the reported strikes. The Guards also did not make clear when the two tankers were allegedly hit, leaving open whether the latest announcements describe new incidents or repeat earlier claims. The reports follow several similar announcements in recent months, many involving unnamed tankers said to have exploded or caught fire while attempting to use shipping routes not authorized by Iran. But assessments from the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) and the Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC) have repeatedly questioned those accounts. In its latest advisory, issued October 18 , JMIC directly addressed Iranian claims that two supertankers struck mines on October 17. “On 17 Oct the IRGC Navy claimed that two supertankers had struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz; there is no substantiation to these claims,” the advisory stated. The assessment, which covered developments through October 18, was issued before Tuesday’s latest statements. The October allegations are not isolated. On July 18, the IRGC claimed two oil tankers exploded and caught fire after entering a minefield in the southern Strait of Hormuz. The Guards accused U.S. intelligence agencies of encouraging the vessels to use the route but did not identify either ship. U.S. Central Command rejected the account as false. A similar claim followed on August 31, when Iranian state television reported that a supertanker had struck two naval mines, caught fire and come to a complete stop while attempting to use the southern passage. CENTCOM issued an unusually direct denial. “No ships have hit mines in the Strait of Hormuz,” the military command said, describing Iran’s announcement as an attempt to intimidate commercial shipping through disinformation. Just two days later, on September 2, the IRGC claimed another two tankers had exploded after striking mines. Again, the ships were not identified. The announcements continued in October. On October 10, Iranian authorities reported that a supertanker carrying approximately 2 million barrels of crude had struck a mine while using an unauthorized southern route. Two days later, the Guards described another incident involving a tanker reportedly carrying 750,000 barrels of crude, calling it a third mine strike. None of those announcements established the identities of the vessels or provided independent confirmation of the cause of the reported explosions. The clearest contradiction emerged last week following the sinking of the Singapore-flagged containership GFS Pride . Iran claimed on October 14 that a containership had struck a naval mine while using an unauthorized route. The description appeared to correspond with GFS Pride , which was attacked on October 13, caught fire and subsequently sank. But JMIC’s October 15 assessment identified the vessel as having been struck by an unknown projectile and explicitly stated that there was no substantiation for Iran’s mine claim. CENTCOM went further, identifying an IRGC projectile as the cause of the attack and saying the containership sank while being towed toward shore. All 21 crew members were safely evacuated. The ship’s sinking left containers and debris floating near the southern approaches to the strait. The lack of confirmation for Iran’s recent mine-strike claims does not mean the waterway is free of mines. In March, Reuters reported that Iran had deployed approximately a dozen naval mines in the strait, citing two sources familiar with the matter. U.S. forces subsequently carried out extensive mine-clearance operations. In late August, President Donald Trump announced that mines had been cleared from the strait’s international shipping lanes, a claim reinforced by CENTCOM commander Adm. Brad Cooper, who said U.S. forces had cleared the internationally recognized traffic separation scheme. However, the possibility of renewed mining remains a concern. JMIC’s October 18 advisory maintains a SEVERE threat level for the Strait of Hormuz and specifically warns mariners to remain vigilant for attempted mining within and adjacent to the traffic separation scheme. That assessment distinguishes a credible threat from a confirmed mine strike. The same advisory documented 153 confirmed maritime security incidents across the wider region since March 1, including attacks involving unidentified projectiles, drones and small boats. UKMTO recorded 12 attacks during the week covered by its October 16 overview. The latest reports include tanker attacks in the Arabian Gulf and a tug struck by two unknown projectiles near Khor Fakkan, UAE, on October 18. The advisory also reported that traffic through Hormuz remained approximately 70% below prewar levels, with 254 vessel transits recorded during the week ending October 14. Iran continues to insist that merchant vessels must follow routes authorized by Tehran, while the United States maintains that international shipping lanes are open and that neutral commercial vessels are entitled to transit. For commercial shipping, the distinction between a confirmed mine strike and an unverified military claim is significant. A verified strike could indicate newly laid mines in waters U.S. forces previously declared clear, potentially requiring renewed clearance operations and changes to voyage planning. For now, maritime security authorities continue to warn of an exceptionally dangerous operating environment, but their public reporting has not substantiated Iran’s latest claims that commercial tankers are being disabled by naval mines. Photo courtesy InterManager A new survey of more than 900 seafarers has exposed a persistent gap between safety procedures and the realities of working aboard ships, prompting renewed calls for action to prevent deaths in enclosed spaces. Ship management association InterManager says it has recorded 354 enclosed space accidents between 1996 and 2026, involving tankers, bulk carriers, containerships, passenger vessels and other ship types. Despite decades of safety campaigns, training requirements and regulatory attention, the association says many of the same problems continue to put seafarers at risk. The latest survey found that crews often struggle with overly complicated procedures, insufficient time and manpower, commercial pressure and inadequate practical training. Respondents also raised concerns that inspections sometimes place more emphasis on paperwork than whether safety measures actually work onboard. “Enclosed spaces have been killing seafarers for decades,” said Captain Kuba Szymanski, InterManager’s secretary general. “The industry does not need more paperwork for the sake of paperwork, it needs practical measures that work onboard.” “If a procedure cannot realistically be completed with the time, people and equipment available, then we need to question the system, not blame the seafarer.” InterManager says the findings point to a need for regular, practical training rather than relying on exercises completed early in a seafarer’s career. Crews should also have a greater say in developing the procedures and systems they are expected to follow. The association is calling for more frequent drills, refresher training, reliable gas detection equipment and effective rescue arrangements. It also sees opportunities to reduce risks through wearable gas monitors, digital entry permits, hands-free communications and remotely operated inspection equipment. Ship design is another concern. InterManager says better equipment placement, improved coatings and more durable piping could reduce the need for crews to enter potentially dangerous spaces in the first place. The findings come as the International Maritime Organization works to strengthen seafarer safety standards. In June 2025, the IMO adopted revised recommendations for entering enclosed spaces, addressing hazard identification, risk assessments and safe entry procedures. The organization is also conducting a broader review of the STCW Convention, with enclosed space training among the issues under consideration. International Maritime Organization +1 InterManager also criticized poor accident reporting and limited information sharing across the industry. The association warned that delayed or incomplete investigations make it harder for operators to learn from previous incidents and prevent similar accidents. “We already know many of the factors behind these accidents. What is missing is consistent action,” Szymanski said. “The priority now must be simpler procedures, better training, stronger leadership, improved ship design and far greater sharing of accident data.” InterManager will discuss the survey findings during a joint webinar with The Nautical Institute on October 27, bringing together maritime safety and human factors experts to examine what needs to change onboard and ashore. “Enclosed space deaths are not inevitable,” Szymanski said. “The industry has the knowledge to prevent them so why isn’t it doing it already?” Sign up for gCaptain’s newsletter and never miss an update Essential maritime and offshore news, insights, and updates delivered daily straight to your inbox Dive into a sea of curated content with our weekly ‘Dispatch’ email. Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said on Monday they launched several attacks on Saudi energy, airport and military targets, such as an Aramco site in Yanbu, the Shaybah oilfield, Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport and Abha airport. Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm the Houthi claims and Reuters could not independently verify them. Brent crude futures fell $1.11, or 1.01%, to $108.44 at 11:36 a.m. ET (1536 GMT). Earlier in the session, the front-month contract reached $111.99, a five-month high. The November contract for US West Texas Intermediate crude, which expires on Tuesday, was down 91 cents, or 0.88%, at $102.75. That was down from the session high of $110.48, the highest since April for a nearby contract. The more active December contract was down 97 cents, or 0.98%, at $97.57 a barrel. "Oil prices remain well-supported. ... This suggests the market is pricing in a significant risk premium, given the situation's volatility," ING analysts said in a note on Tuesday. At least 18 vessels were reportedly attacked over two weeks, which keeps the risk premium intact, shiptracker Kpler said in a note on Monday. Also on Monday, a Houthi attack on a training camp for government security forces in Yemen's Shabwa province killed 58 people and injured more than 200. The renewed attacks heightened fears about regional stability and underscored continuing risks to energy supply from the region, keeping oil prices above $100 a barrel. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said in a statement he is "committed to completing the elimination of the Iranian regime," and spoke with US President Donald Trump about it on Sunday. articles.title: Russian Diesel Cargoes Continue to Intended Destinations After Export Ban Lifts
articles.summary: Russian diesel cargoes are returning to their traditional destinations after the US suspended sanctions and secured the lifting of an export ban, with at least two tankers signalling trips to Turkey and Brazil in recent days, according to shipping data…
articles.body: Russian Diesel Cargoes Continue to Intended Destinations After Export Ban Lifts Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 20, 2026 © Adobe Stock/le Russian diesel cargoes are returning to their traditional destinations after the US suspended sanctions and secured the lifting of an export ban, with at least two tankers signalling trips to Turkey and Brazil in recent days, according to shipping data from Kpler and LSEG. Russia lifted its self-imposed ban on October 9 on diesel exports, introduced to tackle domestic shortages triggered by Ukrainian drone attacks on refineries, after striking a deal with US President Donald Trump to supply diesel to global markets. The deal included a temporary lifting of US sanctions on Russian fuel supply, though EU and UK embargoes on Russian fuel imports remain in force. Trump has set his sights on trying to calm diesel prices ahead of the midterm elections on November 3. Diesel is a key fuel used in industry, agriculture and transportation. Usually the world's second-largest exporter of diesel after the United States, Russia had already reduced its exports in summer before imposing the export ban. RUSSIAN DIESEL EXPORTS DOWN 41% THIS YEAR Total Russian diesel exports were around 345,000 bpd over this year so far, down 41% from last year, the data show. The tanker Leruo was signalling Manaus, Brazil, as its destination after departing from Russia's Baltic port of Primorsk on October 16, the data showed. The tanker Dolunay, which departed Primorsk with a diesel cargo on October 14, is heading for Alanya, Turkey. The two tankers are each carrying 300,000-barrel diesel cargoes, according to Kpler. Morocco has also begun importing Russian diesel since the lifting of the export ban. Turkey has received around 34% of Russian diesel loadings so far this year, Brazil 24% and Morocco 10%, according to Kpler data. ”With Russian supply returning, established trade routes are the most logical place for those barrels to go first. I would also expect Russia to prioritise customers that can absorb meaningful volumes quickly, rather than spend time developing new outlets when global diesel availability remains tight,” said Kpler’s head of geopolitical risk, Michelle Brouhard. Turkish fuel suppliers have reduced purchases of diesel from domestic refineries in anticipation of receiving Russian exports, three sources familiar with the matter told Reuters. Tupras and Socar, which operate Turkey’s major refineries, did not respond to a request for comment. RUSSIA SAYS IT COULD RAISE DIESEL EXPORTS SHARPLY Trump said Russia would immediately export 300,000 metric tons, or 2.25 million barrels, followed by 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter". Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said last week that Russian exports could surpass the levels agreed with Trump, aiming for up to 3.5 million tons per month (875,000 bpd) by the end of the year. The volumes Trump said Russia would supply are modest in comparison to the global shortfall, but at the levels Novak discussed, they would close most of the gap, Sparta Commodities analyst James Noel-Beswick said. Prices of European benchmark diesel futures LGOc1 have not changed significantly since the deal, according to LSEG data, and were trading at an $80 premium to Brent crude LCOc1 on Tuesday. This was off all-time highs of almost $95 in late September, but still several times higher than a year ago. Russian diesel loadings totalled around 210,000 tons, or 1.56 million barrels, over October 11-20, according to Kpler. (Reuters)

REUTERS/Ints Kalnins (Bloomberg) — A US plan to rehabilitate sanctioned tankers to boost oil supply may attract only a sliver of the dark fleet , as existing contracts, complex compliance checks and sky-high freight rates reduce incentives for would-be sellers. The measure — detailed on Monday, just weeks ahead of the US midterm elections — is the latest in a string of efforts by the Trump administration to cool crude and fuel prices driven higher by months of war in the Persian Gulf and the ongoing conflict between Russia and Ukraine. Soaring gasoline and diesel costs in particular have fueled affordability concerns among US voters. But with limited numbers of sanctioned supertankers actually available and would-be sellers unwilling to forgo lucrative crossings in the Middle East, industry analysts say the effort to revive so-called dark vessels may struggle to gain traction. “Sanctions relief does not equal immediately usable mainstream tanker capacity,” said Rahul Kapoor, global head of shipping analytics and research for S&P Global Energy. “The number of vessels that could realistically migrate back into mainstream trading would likely be materially smaller than the overall sanctioned fleet.” Under the US proposal, blacklisted vessels can be sold and rejoin the legitimate fleet, Energy Secretary Chris Wright said on Monday, adding the government would “convert” tankers to expand global availability but would not lift existing sanctions. He did not detail the sale process or potential investors. The US has previously removed vessels from its sanctions list if they met certain conditions. The supertanker Kiara M was blacklisted in December for supporting the Venezuelan oil trade, but was then deleted from the list in March after Washington moved Caracas’s oil trade to the mainstream. A wider plan would meet different hurdles — including the absence of financial incentives to sell up. Even though ships’ resale values have climbed in recent months, soaring freight rates mean that shipowners are still motivated to keep their vessels operating. A supertanker shuttling through the Strait of Hormuz can fetch as much as $40 million per trip, shipbrokers say. That compares to an early October price tag of about $190 million for a 10-year-old vessel, according to Clarksons data. There are also practical challenges, including the simple availability of vessels not already under contract, and the fact that the European Union and the United Kingdom not only also blacklist vessels but also dominate maritime insurance cover, potentially limiting unilateral efforts. Then there is age. Oil Brokerage, an independent energy broker, estimates that there are 294 sanctioned tankers free from EU or UK penalties — but 70% of them are above 20 years old and unpalatable to mainstream traders. That leaves just 75 commercially available tankers of all sizes, including 50 supertankers. “Any capacity return is likely to be gradual rather than immediate,” Oil Brokerage analyst Ting Jun Jie said. Fuel costs have been a pressing concern for the Trump administration, and efforts to cool oil prices over recent months have included periodic waivers on sanctioned oil and a diesel export deal with Russia. Brent remains near a five-month high, however, and a supercharged freight rally shows no signs of slowing. “The administration is doing all these things to bring down prices,” said Karnan Thirupathy, partner at Wotton Kearney who advises clients on sanctions compliance and other regulatory issues on global shipping. “It hadn’t been framed that way in the past. It’s an indication that they’re more inclined to do this more now than before.” © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. articles.title: Iran Strikes More Ship Engine Rooms in Ramp-Up of Hormuz Attacks
articles.summary: Iranian attacks in the Persian Gulf are striking more ships and causing more severe damage than earlier in the conflict, bringing fresh risks to energy flows from the region.

REUTERS/Mohammed Aty (Bloomberg) — Iranian attacks in the Persian Gulf are striking more ships and causing more severe damage than earlier in the conflict , bringing fresh risks to energy flows from the region. At least 23 incidents involving ships attacked in or near the Strait of Hormuz were logged in the first two weeks of October, with at least five reporting impacts to their engine rooms, according to data from naval groups in the region and alerts from security consultants. Direct hits on engine rooms can cause fires and leave ships without power or propulsion, taking vessels out of service for months and leading to costly repairs. Middle Eastern producers have shown a willingness to keep supplying oil in the face of Iranian attacks — preliminary data from trade intelligence company Kpler put the seven-day average of Middle East oil exports fractionally above prewar levels. But the intensifying strikes threaten to worsen one of the biggest constraints in the global oil market: the number of available ships. Several shipping and maritime security officials, speaking on condition of anonymity because of the sensitive nature of the topic, said they were seeing increased levels of engine-room damage from attacks, as well as a larger volume of incidents in general, but that it was hard to say if Iran was deliberately targeting ship engines. “What we’re seeing is an increase in the frequency of attacks, and therefore, more damage in engine rooms and disabling fire,” said Phillip Belcher, marine director at Intertanko, the world’s main trade group for the tanker industry. Persistent strikes on engines invoke memories of the 1980s Tanker War, when Iraq and Iran targeted oil tankers’ engine rooms in an effort to disable them. Some attacks caused fires and explosions that ultimately sank vessels. Dozens of damaged or sunken ships remained in the northern Gulf for years after. At least two recently-hit vessels sank last week, including a container ship that was struck in Hormuz. After the container ship sank, Pakistan’s Hydrographic Services said there were containers floating adrift near the United Arab Emirates. There were no attacks leading to engine damage in September, according to the data, and at least seven on non-Iranian vessels in previous months. When enforcing its blockade on Iranian ships, the US has also targeted engine rooms in order to disable vessels. Iran has recently begun using more missiles, rather than drones, to hit vessels, the shipping and maritime security officials said. Infrared-guided missiles tend to steer towards hotter parts of the ship, and often have larger explosive payloads than drones. For now, flows are continuing through the Strait of Hormuz, though estimates vary. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said on Sunday that shipments are at about 80% of normal levels, and Iraq said Monday that its own exports are approaching prewar levels. But attacks on engine rooms will do little to draw owners back to Hormuz, and ships that come under attack remain out of action for longer as they undergo repairs. That could further restrict the number of tankers available to carry barrels, and push up the price of transporting energy. For a few days this month it was more expensive to hire a supertanker in some parts of the world than it was to send a rocket into space. “In a region where few owners are willing to put ships in, every VLCC hit is material,” analysts at Oil Brokerage Ltd. said in a note on Oct. 19, referring to very large crude carriers. Risks to the seafarers employed by shipping companies to sail through the region are also growing. One recent attack on a bulk commodity carrier struck the bridge and accommodation area where crew sleep, according to a report from the Joint Maritime Information Center, which distributes information on maritime security in the region. “Attacks often focus on the engine room or the bridge of the ships as it maximizes damage while keeping the risk of an oil spill relatively low,” said Jakob Larsen, chief safety and security officer at Bimco, the world’s largest shipping trade group. “Sadly, there are significant risks of crew injuries when these areas of the ship are hit.” © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. articles.summary: Maritime data provider Kpler has reached an agreement with Airbus to expand its ability to track vessels that disappear from conventional ship-tracking systems, adding daily satellite imagery to help identify...

SPOT © CNES 2026, Distribution Airbus DS/Handout via REUTERS Maritime data provider Kpler has reached an agreement with Airbus to expand its ability to track vessels that disappear from conventional ship-tracking systems, adding daily satellite imagery to help identify ships operating without reliable Automatic Identification System (AIS) signals. The agreement, announced Tuesday , will integrate imagery from Airbus’s SPOT Earth observation satellites with Kpler’s existing vessel-tracking network, allowing analysts to detect ships independently of their reported AIS positions. The service will use high-resolution satellite imagery, with a resolution of 1.5 meters and a 60-kilometer swath, combined with artificial intelligence to identify vessels at sea and in port. The technology is intended to address a growing challenge for maritime tracking: determining whether a vessel has deliberately switched off or manipulated its AIS signal, or whether its reported position has been affected by interference with satellite navigation systems. That distinction has become increasingly important as AIS spoofing, GPS jamming and other forms of electronic interference complicate vessel tracking in major shipping corridors, particularly around conflict zones. While some vessels deliberately manipulate their positions to conceal movements, others may report inaccurate locations because of widespread Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) interference affecting multiple ships in the same area. By comparing AIS data with independently captured satellite imagery, Kpler says it can better distinguish between the two. “No single data source tells the whole story,” said Jean-Charles Gordon, Kpler’s vice president of maritime and logistics. Gordon said combining AIS information with satellite imagery and other independent sources would give shipping companies and governments a clearer picture of maritime activity, particularly when vessels disappear from electronic tracking systems. The expanded capability could also prove useful in monitoring sanctions evasion and so-called shadow fleet operations, where vessels sometimes manipulate or disable AIS transmissions to obscure their movements. In an earlier analysis of AIS spoofing and GNSS interference , Kpler identified the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz, Black Sea, Baltic Sea and Red Sea among the maritime regions affected by navigation-signal interference. The company has also highlighted the importance of distinguishing deliberate AIS manipulation from external interference when assessing sanctions compliance and marine insurance risks. AIS remains the primary means of tracking commercial shipping, transmitting information including a vessel’s position, speed, course and destination. Kpler says its existing network collects billions of AIS messages daily. The Airbus partnership adds another source of information that does not depend on those transmissions, potentially allowing analysts to verify a vessel’s actual location even when its electronic track is missing or misleading. The companies did not disclose financial terms or specify when the expanded detection service would become fully operational. articles.summary: Iran has deliberately prolonged talks with the US to try to weaken Donald Trump politically ahead of November's US midterm elections, senior officials say, while fears of renewed military action and deep distrust of Washington have reinforced Tehran's reluctance to strike a quick deal to end the war.
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network Vessels in the Strait of Hormuz near the beach of Bandar Abbas, Iran, September 28, 2026. Amirhosein Khorgooi/ISNA/via WANA (West Asia News Agency) via REUTERS DUBAI, Oct 20 (Reuters) – Iran has deliberately prolonged talks with the US to try to weaken Donald Trump politically ahead of November’s US midterm elections, senior officials say, while fears of renewed military action and deep distrust of Washington have reinforced Tehran’s reluctance to strike a quick deal to end the war . Three senior Iranian officials and an Iranian insider, speaking on condition of anonymity, said Tehran was convinced the US president was ready to resort to renewed attacks to try to break the stalemate in the eight-month-old war. “Iran is preparing for renewed Israeli and US attacks, not for a deal with America to end the war,” one of the officials said. “The clerical establishment is determined not to give Trump a political victory.” Tehran analyst Saeed Leylaz said that, by prolonging the talks, “Iran is influencing the US election without taking any unlawful action.” The war, which began in February when the US and its ally Israel launched strikes on Iran, has helped drive Trump’s approval rating to a record low as polls suggest that Americans worried about high gasoline prices will punish his Republican Party in the November 3 congressional elections. Trump has repeatedly said he expects oil prices to drop after the elections, but has not offered a detailed plan to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, a vital global energy shipping route effectively closed by Iran since the war began. Iranian attacks both threatened and real have kept ship traffic through the strait to a trickle, while a US maritime blockade and trade sanctions have cut off Iran’s oil export revenues and exacerbated growing domestic economic woes. With Tehran refusing to make concessions it believes could benefit Trump politically, there is little chance of a breakthrough before the elections, the officials said. Under pressure from Israel, Washington wants Iran’s decades-long nuclear program – which Iran says is purely peaceful and Western powers allege has military dimensions – on the table from the outset. For its part, Tehran insists that its conditions under a “seven-day plan” must be met before nuclear negotiations begin. And it offers no prospect of giving up the leverage over the Strait of Hormuz that the conflict prompted it to seize. Iran’s Foreign Ministry and the US White House did not respond to Reuters requests for comment. Iran’s proposal, conveyed through Qatari mediators, offered to reopen the strait within seven days, albeit under Iranian control, provided that Washington lifted its maritime blockade, eased restrictions on Iranian oil exports, released frozen assets and ended hostilities on all fronts. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said on Sunday that the offer remained on the table, with messages being exchanged through mediators. Tehran’s view that Washington cannot be trusted to commit to diplomacy stems from the attacks on Iran that have derailed previous negotiations, one Iranian official said. In June 2025, an Israeli attack wrecked plans for a sixth round of US-Iran nuclear talks in Oman. And last February, the US and Israel launched their war just after another round of talks ended, with further technical discussions scheduled. Maintaining a state somewhere between war and peace through the US midterms allows Iran to sustain pressure on Washington while reiterating its commitment to diplomacy. Trump has said the US will not bomb Iran again before November 3. However, the officials said Tehran continues to expect that bombing will resume, sooner or later. Alex Vatanka, director of the Iran program at the Middle East Institute in Washington, said the clerical establishment clearly wanted to hurt Trump politically. “But the fundamental issue is that Tehran believes that Trump is interested in regime change … and following Israeli Prime Minister (Benjamin) Netanyahu’s policy of seeking to bring down Iran’s ruling establishment,” he said. US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth discussed Iran with Netanyahu on Monday, three Israeli officials said, in an unannounced visit to Israel a week before a parliamentary election in which Netanyahu’s position is at risk. Iran’s strategy of keeping negotiations alive without rushing towards agreement comes at a cost. Prolonged uncertainty is weighing on Iran’s already crippled economy and wearing down public patience. Thousands were killed at the turn of the year when the security forces crushed spiraling anti-government protests. Annual inflation hit 73.6% in September, according to the Statistical Centre of Iran, and the rial currency has fallen nearly 35% against the dollar since Washington reapplied its naval blockade in July. Iran’s seaborne crude exports fell to zero in the second week of September from a 14-day average of 230,000 barrels per day at the start of the month, and remained there as of October 5, according to energy intelligence platform Vortexa. But the leadership’s distrust of Washington extends beyond the current conflict to existential concerns. Iran believes the US has repeatedly broken agreements even when Tehran honored its commitments, Leylaz said, leaving little confidence that any comprehensive deal would endure. “Reaching a sustainable deal with the US, even after the Trump administration, is no longer possible because of the deepened distrust,” Leylaz said. “Nothing will go back to the pre-war status quo.” (Writing by Parisa Hafezi; Additional reporting by Steve Holland in Washington; Editing by Kevin Liffey) (c) Copyright Thomson Reuters 2026. articles.title: Fairbanks Morse Defense Breaks Ground on New Center of Excellence
articles.summary: Fairbanks Morse Defense (FMD) broke ground on a third Center of Excellence (CoE3) at the Bird-Johnson Propeller Company facility in Pascagoula, Miss. The new center will effectively double capacity to produce complex and powerful naval propulsion…
articles.body: Fairbanks Morse Defense Breaks Ground on New Center of Excellence Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 20, 2026 © Fairbanks Morse Defense Fairbanks Morse Defense (FMD) broke ground on a third Center of Excellence (CoE3) at the Bird-Johnson Propeller Company facility in Pascagoula, Miss. The new center will effectively double capacity to produce complex and powerful naval propulsion systems. The $60 million installation includes a $27 million U.S. Navy investment, $22 million of which is sourced from Australia’s initial contribution to the U.S. Submarine Industrial Base (SIB) under the AUKUS Pillar I effort. CoE3 will complement existing foundry capacity with the addition of 38,000 square feet of new manufacturing space, two new five-axis computer numerical control (CNC) machines equipped for parts weighing up to 100 metric tons (approximately 220,000 lbs.) and a machine-ready expansion slot for further growth. This capability will address current maritime industry capacity constraints and support submarine production and fleet readiness. The Pascagoula foundry upgrade will grow the workforce by 25%, employing a total of 100 highly skilled craftspeople. Once complete, CoE3 will support FMD training and apprenticeship programs and create new opportunities in high-tech manufacturing to strengthen the Gulf Coast economy and restore America’s defense industrial base. The addition of two new five-axis CNC machines with 7-meter turntables brings the total machine count to four. CoE3 also modernizes legacy foundry capabilities with a dedicated manufacturing bay for a future 3D sand printer. The current and future design establishes a versatile, fully integrated manufacturing hub that encompasses design and casting through machining, finishing and delivery. As the only privately-owned U.S. foundry certified for large-scale Navy propeller manufacturing, the Pascagoula facility is designated a U.S. National Asset. The center will be operated as a Bird-Johnson Propeller Company facility under the executive leadership of Fairbanks Morse Defense. FMD acquired Bird-Johnson in July 2025 and restored the Bird-Johnson name to the foundry, honoring the company’s nearly 70-year commitment to American-made naval propellers. The official groundbreaking coincides with America’s 250th anniversary, with new capacity scheduled to come online by Q1 2028.

Join the leading maritime news network Photo courtesy European Commission The European Union unveiled a new Arctic strategy Tuesday aimed at strengthening maritime security, expanding icebreaker capacity and protecting critical infrastructure as melting sea ice opens new shipping routes and geopolitical competition intensifies across the region. The strategy , the EU’s first major update since 2021, marks a shift toward security and economic interests in a region increasingly important to global shipping, trade and energy supplies. At the center of the plan is a proposed Maritime Security Hub designed to improve surveillance and information sharing across the Arctic, including the monitoring and protection of critical undersea infrastructure. “The Arctic is one place where the tectonic plates of geopolitics are colliding,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Tuesday in Strasbourg. Von der Leyen pointed to Russia’s growing military presence in the Arctic, increasing pressure on regional security and the emergence of new shipping routes as reasons for Europe to take a more active role. “When we see Russia rebuilding its Arctic military footprint, pursuing hybrid strategies against the neighbors, and reshaping the security of the Arctic, it impacts the European Union as a whole,” she said. The new strategy comes as Russia, China, the United States and European countries compete for influence in the Arctic, where retreating sea ice is changing access to shipping lanes and natural resources. Maritime Security and Icebreakers Take Priority Under the plan, the EU will work with member states and Arctic partners to establish a Maritime Security Hub that brings together surveillance and monitoring information from satellites, vessels and seabed infrastructure. An Arctic Cable Hub would be an initial component, helping authorities monitor, protect and coordinate repairs to submarine cables across the North Atlantic and Arctic. The EU also plans to expand its use of satellite monitoring and data sharing, including a dedicated Arctic surveillance pilot scheduled for 2027 to improve maritime domain awareness. Icebreakers are another priority. The Commission said it will assess Europe’s shipbuilding capabilities and operational requirements while supporting joint procurement and resource sharing to increase the availability of advanced icebreakers. The effort reflects growing recognition that operating in the Arctic requires specialized vessels and infrastructure, even as sea ice retreats. Beyond security, the strategy calls for better integration of European ports, rail connections, energy terminals and digital infrastructure into emerging Arctic trade networks. The EU also wants to strengthen connectivity through a proposed Pan-Arctic submarine cable linking Greenland directly to Europe, with potential future extensions to Canada and Japan. Secure satellite communications would be supported by the EU’s IRIS² program, while a new ocean monitoring initiative known as OceanEye would improve data sharing, maritime safety and climate observations. A Changing Arctic Shipping Landscape The strategy comes as Arctic shipping draws increasing interest from governments and commercial operators seeking alternative connections between Europe and Asia. Russia has invested heavily in developing its Northern Sea Route along its Arctic coastline, while China has expanded its interest in polar shipping and infrastructure. For Europe, the changing Arctic presents both an economic opportunity and a security challenge. New shipping routes could create opportunities for ports, logistics providers and shipbuilders, but Arctic operations remain constrained by ice conditions, limited infrastructure, environmental risks and the availability of emergency response capabilities. The Commission said its approach will emphasize cooperation with Arctic partners, including Norway, Iceland, Canada, the United Kingdom and the United States, while complementing NATO’s role in regional security. The strategy also maintains the EU’s focus on climate change. The Arctic is warming nearly four times faster than the global average, according to the Commission, with consequences for sea ice, ecosystems and coastal communities. The EU reaffirmed its opposition to hydrocarbon development that threatens Arctic ecosystems, although the new strategy drops a previous commitment to pursue an international legal ban on new Arctic oil and gas development. Alongside security and economic development, the plan includes expanded polar research, investment in regional infrastructure and greater involvement of Arctic communities and Indigenous Peoples. More than half a million EU citizens live in Arctic regions of Denmark, Finland and Sweden. The Commission did not attach an overall price tag to the new strategy, leaving questions about how quickly some of the proposed security, shipping and infrastructure projects will move forward. Still, the new framework makes clear that Brussels increasingly views the Arctic not only as an environmental priority, but also as an important region for Europe’s maritime security, trade and economic interests. articles.title: Steerprop to Provide Ice-Class Propulsion for Danish Multi-Role Environmental Vessel
articles.summary: Finnish marine propulsion provider Steerprop has secured a contract with Karstensens Skibsværft to supply a complete ice-class propulsion package for a Multi-Role Environmental Vessel being built for the Royal Danish Navy.The vessel is one of…
articles.body: Steerprop to Provide Ice-Class Propulsion for Danish Multi-Role Environmental Vessel Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 20, 2026 The new Multi-Role Environmental Vessel being built for the Royal Danish Navy by Karstensens Skibsværft will be equipped with two Steerprop SP 45 W azimuth propulsors and a Steerprop SP 10 TT tunnel thruster. Image: OSK Design. Finnish marine propulsion provider Steerprop has secured a contract with Karstensens Skibsværft to supply a complete ice-class propulsion package for a Multi-Role Environmental Vessel being built for the Royal Danish Navy. The vessel is one of four commissioned by the Danish Ministry of Defence Acquisition and Logistics Organisation to strengthen Denmark's marine environmental response and defense capabilities. The program is being delivered by Orlogsskibe Danmark, a consortium comprising OSK Design, Karstensens Skibsværft and Hvide Sande Shipyard. The project marks an important milestone for Steerprop, demonstrating the company's capability to deliver propulsion control systems compliant with DNV's SP2 cyber security requirements. Steerprop's will deliver two Steerprop SP 45 W azimuth propulsors rated at 2,200 kW each – including permanent-magnet motors also supplied by Steerpop - together with a Steerprop SP 10 TT tunnel thruster rated at 750 kW. The scope also includes bridge control systems and the complete propulsion control system. The integrated propulsion package is designed to support the vessel's DNV Ice Class 1A notation, enabling reliable operation in demanding ice conditions. Steerprop's W series azimuth propulsors combine advanced drivetrain design with highly efficient hydrodynamics to deliver reliable performance in some of the world's most demanding operating environments. The optimized housing geometry and robust cast-steel lower unit maximize efficiency, durability and operational reliability. The design has already proven itself in commercial applications ranging from harbour tugs to heavy-duty offshore vessels operating in demanding ice conditions. Steerprop has supplied mission-critical propulsion systems for governmental and naval vessel programs worldwide, including projects in Canada, the United States and across the Nordic and Baltic regions. Through these projects, the company has developed extensive expertise in meeting the demanding operational, technical and lifecycle requirements of naval and government operators. Construction of the vessel series has already begun at Karstensens Skibsværft's yard in Gdańsk, Poland. Steerprop will begin deliveries of the propulsion package in March 2027, with the first vessel expected to enter service in 2029.
